# Patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases remain at risk for hospitalisation for COVID-19 infection in the Omicron era (2022–2024): a retrospective cohort study

**Authors:** Naomi J Patel; Shruthi Srivatsan; Emily N Kowalski; Andrew King; Xiaosong Wang; Kathleen MM Vanni; Grace Qian; Jennifer S Hanberg; Katarina J Bade; Alene A Saavedra; Kevin T Mueller; Buuthien Hang; Zachary K Williams; Colebrooke Johnson; Madison Negron; Jeffrey A Sparks; Zachary S Wallace

**Affiliations:** 1Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 2Rheumatology Unit, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3Department of Medicine, Division of Rheumatology, Inflammation, and Immunity, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 4Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

To investigate the risk factors for severe acute COVID-19 outcomes in the Omicron era among individuals with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs).

We identified patients with confirmed SARDs and COVID-19 (positive PCR and/or antigen test) from 1 September 2022 to 15 March 2024 in the Mass General Brigham healthcare system. We estimated the associations of baseline characteristics with the odds of hospitalisation due to COVID-19 infection, verified by medical record review, using multivariable logistic regression.

Of 2061 patients with SARDs and COVID-19 during the Omicron era (75% female, mean age 62.2 years), 134 (6.5%) were hospitalised due to COVID-19, mostly due to respiratory symptoms (84, 63%). Of those hospitalised, 11 (8%) required mechanical ventilation and 20 (15%) died. Older age (adjusted OR (aOR) 1.05 per year), Black race (vs White race, aOR 4.15), ever smoking (vs never, aOR 1.76), CD20 inhibitor use (vs antimalarial monotherapy, aOR 2.22) and glucocorticoid use (vs non-use, aOR 2.07) were significantly associated with higher odds of hospitalisation. Female sex (vs male, aOR 0.63), booster SARS-CoV-2 vaccination (vs initial series, aOR 0.49) and vaccination within either 3 months or 3–6 months prior to infection (aOR 0.41 and aOR 0.38, respectively, vs none within 12 months) were significantly associated with lower odds of hospitalisation.

Some patients with SARDs remain at higher risk of severe COVID-19 in the Omicron era. Patients who are older, Black, have more comorbidities, use CD20 inhibitors and/or glucocorticoids, or have not been vaccinated recently may benefit from risk-mitigating strategies, including booster vaccines and pre-exposure prophylaxis.

Keywords: COVID-19, Autoimmune Diseases, Glucocorticoids, Rituximab, Vaccination

## WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

- Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, certain demographic and disease-specific factors, as well as use of CD20 inhibitors and systemic glucocorticoids, were associated with higher risk of severe acute COVID-19, but less is known about the contemporary epidemiology in patients with rheumatic disease

- Immunosuppressive medications are associated with impaired response to SARS-CoV-2 vaccines.

## WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS

- In the Omicron era, Black race was associated with higher odds of hospitalisation compared with White race.

- CD20 inhibitor and systemic glucocorticoid use remain significant risk factors for hospitalisation due to COVID-19 infection.

- Additional SARS-CoV-2 vaccine doses (beyond two mRNA vaccines or one adenovirus vaccine) and more recent vaccination (within 6 months prior to COVID-19 infection) were associated with significantly lower odds of severe COVID-19.

## HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

- Our data indicate that some individuals with SARDs remain at particularly high risk of hospitalisation and death from COVID-19 during the Omicron era and may benefit from specific counselling and mitigating strategies

- Updated booster vaccines should continue to be recommended for those at high risk of severe outcomes.

## Introduction

Since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, there has been a temporal decline in the risk of death and other severe outcomes (eg, hospitalisation, mechanical ventilation) in the general population and among people with rheumatic disease.1 Since December 2021, Omicron variants have been the dominant circulating strains, with the KP.2, KP.3 and LB.1 variants having the highest current prevalence in the USA as of August 2024.2 Data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention indicate a >60% reduction in hospitalisations for COVID-19 infection since 2021 and a marked reduction in deaths due to COVID-19.3 Similarly, among individuals with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs), we reported that those infected during the Omicron era had over a threefold lower odds of hospitalisation compared with those infected in the early pandemic.1

While COVID-19 outcomes have improved, factors associated with severe COVID-19 among individuals with SARDs in the Omicron era—during which >95% of the population has antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 and in which multiple treatments are available—remain unclear.2 Since the early pandemic, individuals with SARDs have been identified as having increased risk of COVID-19 infection and severe outcomes because of immunosuppressive medication use, comorbidity burdens and immune dysregulation.4,13 Multiple medications that are regularly used to treat immune-mediated diseases, including CD20 inhibitors, glucocorticoids and several conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), have been associated with impaired humoral response to SARS-CoV-2 and other vaccines, risk of breakthrough infection and/or risk of more severe outcome of acute COVID-19 infection.14,21 Therefore, we investigated the risk factors for severe outcomes among individuals with SARDs and COVID-19 in a large healthcare system in the USA during the Omicron era.

## Methods

### Study population and design

We performed a retrospective cohort study investigating the factors associated with severe outcomes of acute COVID-19 among patients with SARDs in a large healthcare system. Mass General Brigham (MGB) is a multicentre healthcare system that includes a total of 14 hospitals, including 2 tertiary care hospitals (Massachusetts General Hospital and Brigham and Women’s Hospital), as well as other primary care and specialty outpatient centres in the greater Boston, Massachusetts, area. We identified adult patients with manually confirmed SARD diagnoses and COVID-19 infection based on our previously described methods involving identification of individuals from positive SARS-CoV-2 tests, including those done at home, and/or COVID-19 antiviral prescription in the electronic health record (EHR). Individuals with a positive home COVID-19 test who communicate the test result to any provider are also identified with a COVID-19 flag in the EHR and are included in this study.

### Patient and public involvement

Patients and/or the public were not involved in the design, or conduct, or reporting, or dissemination plans of this research

### Exposures of interest

Details of demographics, including age, self-reported race, SARD diagnoses and treatment, COVID-19 infection history and SARS-CoV-2 vaccination history (including number and type of doses as well as timing of most recent dose in relation to COVID-19 infection), were extracted from our ongoing registry of individuals with SARDs and COVID-19 infection. These details are manually extracted from the EHR. Comorbidity data (which were used to calculate the Charlson Comorbidity Index) and body mass index were extracted from the MGB Research Patient Data Registry as previously described using ICD-10 codes and vital sign data, respectively.22 23 Blocks of calendar time were determined based on the four waves of infections in Massachusetts within the study period and were as follows: (1) 1 September 2022 to 30 November 2022; (2) 1 December 2022 to 30 April 2023; (3) 1 May 2023 to 31 October 2023; and (4) 1 November 2023 to 15 March 2024.24 September 2022 was chosen as the start of the study period given that this is when the first bivalent vaccine became available.25

For the purpose of categorising patients into a single, mutually exclusive medication group, antimalarial monotherapy was used as the reference group. As we have done previously, for those on multiple medications, the order of precedence in terms of categorising patients into a single group was as follows: CD20 inhibitor, cyclophosphamide, tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor, interleukin (IL)-6 inhibitor, CTLA-4 inhibitor, IL-17A inhibitor/IL-23 inhibitor/IL-12/23 inhibitor, other bDMARD, targeted synthetic DMARD (tsDMARD)/JAK inhibitor, mycophenolate mofetil or mycophenolic acid, methotrexate, then other conventional synthetic DMARD (csDMARD).

### Outcome assessment: hospitalisation due to COVID-19 infection

The primary outcome was hospitalisation due to the first COVID-19 infection within the study period (1 September 2022 to 15 March 2024) which corresponds to the time period when Omicron was the predominant variant in Massachusetts, USA.26 Hospitalisation due to COVID-19 was defined as hospitalisation within 30 days of a COVID-19 diagnosis that was determined to be related to COVID-19 infection based on manual chart review by a physician study team member. Individuals either found to incidentally have COVID-19 on admission and/or those with nosocomial infection who were hospitalised for unrelated reasons were not considered to be hospitalised due to COVID-19. For those hospitalised, we also evaluated the details of hospitalisation, including duration of hospitalisation, level of respiratory support provided and death within 90 days of COVID-19 diagnosis. Deaths were also reviewed by a study physician (NJP) to determine their relation to COVID-19 infection.

A secondary outcome was severe hospitalisation, defined as a requirement of either low-flow supplemental oxygen, non-invasive ventilation or high-flow oxygen, or invasive mechanical ventilation, and/or death within 90 days that was due to COVID-19. These categories correspond to levels 4–8 from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Ordinal Scale for COVID-19 severity, with levels 1–3 indicating no hospitalisation or hospitalisation without any supplemental oxygen requirement.27

### Statistical analysis

Categorical variables are presented as number (percentage), and continuous variables are presented as mean±SD or median±IQR, as appropriate. Each individual’s first COVID-19 infection within the study period was considered.

We evaluated the association between exposures of interest among individuals with SARDs and COVID-19 with the odds of hospitalisation due to COVID-19 using unadjusted and multivariable-adjusted logistic regression to estimate ORs and 95% CIs. The multivariable model was adjusted for age, sex, race, calendar time and Charlson Comorbidity Index given that these are factors that have been identified as being associated with increased risk of adverse outcomes of COVID-19 infection.28,31 We also assessed the association of baseline exposures with severe hospitalisation, our secondary outcome of interest.

To assess the robustness of our results, we performed two sensitivity analyses in which we limited the study population to those with rheumatoid arthritis and (1) used methotrexate as the reference group and (2) TNF inhibitor as the reference group in the immunomodulatory medication analysis. These approaches were used to further address the risk of confounding by indication. We additionally performed subgroup analyses in those who were vaccinated versus unvaccinated against SARS-CoV-2.

The level of significance was set as a two-tailed p<0.05, and statistical analyses were completed using SAS statistical software (V.9.4; SAS Institute, Inc, Cary, North Carolina, USA). A forest plot was created in R using tidyverse/ggplot2.

## Results

### Study sample

We identified 2061 patients with a SARD diagnosis and COVID-19 infection between 1 September 2022 and 15 March 2024 (figure 1). The mean (SD) age was 62.2±15.7 years and 1541 (74.5%) were female (table 1). Most patients identified as White race (1726, 85.8%), followed by Black race (109, 5.4%). The most common comorbidities included hypertension (898, 43.6%), diabetes (271, 13.2%), asthma (269, 13.1%) and cancer (230, 11.2%). The most common SARDs were rheumatoid arthritis (793, 38.5%), other inflammatory arthritis (228, 11.1%), systemic lupus erythematosus (211, 10.2%) and giant cell arteritis and/or polymyalgia rheumatica (162, 7.9%).

Among all patients, 239 (11.6%) were on antimalarial monotherapy. Other frequently used medications in this cohort included TNF inhibitors (439, 21.3%), methotrexate (318, 15.4%), CD20 inhibitors (169, 8.2%), IL-6 receptor inhibitors (95, 4.6%) or other biologic DMARDs (97, 4.7%). Of the 97 on ‘other biologic DMARDs’, 30 were on secukinumab, 19 were on ixekizumab, 18 were on ustekinumab, 13 were on belimumab, 6 were on risankizumab, 5 were on anifrolumab, 3 were on anakinra, 2 were on rilonacept and 1 was on guselkumab. 453 (22.0%) were on no immunomodulatory medications at the time of COVID-19 onset. Overall, 457 (22.2%) were using glucocorticoids at the time of infection, with a median (IQR) prednisone-equivalent dose of 5 (5, 10) mg daily (table 1).

The distribution of calendar time of COVID-19 infections was varied, with 431 (20.9%) occurring from 1 September 2022 to 30 November 2022; 675 (32.7%) occurring from 1 December 2022 to 30 April 2023; 572 (27.7%) occurring from 1 May 2023 to 31 October 2023; and 384 (18.6%) occurring from 1 November 2023 to 15 March 2024.

The vast majority (1965, 95.3%) of patients were vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2 prior to their COVID-19 infection during the Omicron era; 582 (28.2%) had received the initial series (either two mRNA vaccines or one adenovirus vaccine), and the remainder (1383, 67.1%) had received at least one additional dose. 644 patients (31.2%) had not received any SARS-CoV-2 vaccine in the 12 months prior to infection, while most (1,420; 68.8%) were vaccinated within 12 months. A total of 596 (28.9%) had received a vaccine within 6–12 months, 341 (16.5%) had received a vaccine between 3 and 6 months prior to infection and 391 (19.0%) had received a dose within 3 months of infection.

### Description of hospitalisations for COVID-19

Among 2061 individuals, 155 (7.5%) were hospitalised within 30 days of their first positive test for COVID-19 during the study period (figure 1); 21 of these hospitalisations were for reasons unrelated to COVID-19 infection (eg, small bowel obstruction, osteomyelitis of the foot, postprocedural rectus sheath haematoma). Thus, 134 individuals (6.5%) were hospitalised due to their first COVID-19 infection within the study period. Figure 1 illustrates the identification of individuals with SARDs and COVID-19 infection, the review of individuals who were hospitalised, and the exclusion of those who were hospitalised for reasons unrelated to COVID-19 infection or who were not hospitalised for their first COVID-19 infection within the study period.

The reasons for hospitalisation included respiratory COVID-19 symptoms (84, 62.7%), non-respiratory COVID-19 symptoms (27, 20.2%), acute kidney injury (7, 5.2%), post-viral bacterial pneumonia (7, 5.2%) or other COVID-19 complications (9, 6.7%), such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and/or asthma exacerbation, organising pneumonia, supraglottitis, neutropenia, adrenal crisis and cardiac arrest. The median (IQR) length of hospital stay was 5 (3, 10) days (table 2). Of those hospitalised, 61 (45.5%) did not require any supplemental oxygen, 52 (38.8%) required low-flow supplemental oxygen, 10 (7.5%) required non-invasive ventilation or high-flow oxygen and 11 (8.2%) required mechanical ventilation. The majority (119, 88.8%) received treatment for COVID-19, including remdesivir (102, 76.1%), glucocorticoids (47, 35.1%), nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (21, 15.7%) or molnupiravir (2, 1.5%).

### Factors associated with hospitalisation for COVID-19 during the Omicron era

In both unadjusted and multivariable models, older age (adjusted OR (aOR) 1.05 per year, 95% CI: 1.04 to 1.07), back race (aOR 4.15 compared with White race, 95% CI: 2.30 to 7.51), higher Charlson Comorbidity Index (aOR 2.05 per unit, 95% CI: 1.52 to 2.76), ever smoking (aOR 1.76 compared with never smoking, 95% CI: 1.20 to 2.60) and several specific comorbidities, including hypertension, diabetes, coronary artery disease, malignancy, end-stage renal disease and interstitial lung disease, were each associated with higher odds of hospitalisation (figure 2; Online supplemental table 1).

Female sex (aOR 0.63 compared with male sex, 95% CI: 0.43 to 0.93) and additional SARS-CoV-2 vaccines beyond the initial primary series (aOR 0.49 compared with initial vaccine series, 95% CI: 0.33 to 0.72) were associated with lower odds of hospitalisation. Receipt of a SARS-CoV-2 vaccine within the 3 months prior to COVID-19 infection (aOR 0.41, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.75) or 3–6 months prior to COVID-19 infection (aOR 0.38, 95% CI: 0.20 to 0.72) were associated with lower odds of hospitalisation compared with no vaccine within 12 months of infection.

Compared with those on antimalarial monotherapy, those on CD20 inhibitors had significantly higher odds of hospitalisation (aOR 2.22, 95% CI: 1.02 to 4.81). Systemic glucocorticoid use at the time of infection was also associated with higher odds of hospitalisation (aOR 2.07 compared with no glucocorticoid use, 95% CI: 1.41 to 3.04). No other DMARD use was associated with significantly higher odds of hospitalisation compared with those on antimalarial monotherapy (figure 2; Online supplemental table 1).

There was no association of calendar time over the study period with hospitalisation for COVID-19. History of COVID-19 infection in the 12 months prior to infection (n=63) was associated with a numerically lower risk of severe infection (aOR 0.53 vs those with no prior COVID-19 in the past 12 months, 95% CI: 0.12 to 2.39) but did not achieve statistical significance.

### Secondary analyses

When defining the outcome as severe hospitalisation (ie, any oxygen requirement and/or death within 90 days due to COVID-19), we found that older age, Black race, smoking, CCI, CD20 inhibitor use and systemic glucocorticoid use remained significantly associated with higher odds of the outcome, and that additional SARS-CoV-2 vaccines beyond the initial series and more recent SARS-CoV-2 vaccination were associated with lower odds (online supplemental table 2).

Among individuals with rheumatoid arthritis (n=793), those using CD20 inhibitors had significantly higher odds of hospitalisation (aOR 4.52, 95% CI: 1.44 to 14.13) compared with those using methotrexate. Systemic glucocorticoid use at the time of infection was associated with higher odds of hospitalisation (aOR 3.01 compared with no glucocorticoid use, 95% CI: 1.64 to 5.54) (online supplemental table 3). When using a reference group of individuals using TNF inhibitors, those using CD20 inhibitors still had higher odds of hospitalisation (aOR 3.14, 95% CI: 1.07 to 9.25) (online supplemental table 4). Other associations (older age, greater comorbidity burden, Black race, additional SARS-CoV-2 vaccine and more recent vaccination in the 6 months prior to infection) persisted in these analyses limited to patients with rheumatoid arthritis (online supplemental table 3 and 4). Being unvaccinated is more highly associated with hospitalisation among those with rheumatoid arthritis (aOR 3.00 vs those who received the initial vaccine series, 95% CI: 1.04 to 8.64) versus those with all SARDs.

Among those who were vaccinated (n=1965), we found similar results, with significant associations of age, sex, Black race, comorbidities and glucocorticoid use with hospitalisation (online supplemental table 5). CD20 inhibitor use was numerically but not significantly associated with hospitalisation in this cohort (aOR 2.08, 95% CI: 0.94 to 4.57). Among individuals who were unvaccinated (n=96) (online supplemental table 6), many analyses were limited due to small sample size; of the analyses able to be performed, there was no significant association between age, sex or race with hospitalisation for COVID-19.

## Discussion

In this large, multicentre retrospective cohort study of patients with SARDs and COVID-19 infection during the Omicron era, we identified modifiable and non-modifiable factors associated with hospitalisation for COVID-19. In particular, older age, Black race, higher comorbidity burden and either CD20 inhibitor or systemic glucocorticoid use at the time of infection were associated with higher risk of hospitalisation, including severe hospitalisation. Further, we found that female sex and SARS-CoV-2 booster doses reduced the odds of severe COVID-19. We did not find a decrease in odds of hospitalisation throughout calendar time over the 18-month study period. Collectively, these findings highlight the ongoing risk that many patients with SARDs still face, even in an era with vaccines, antiviral therapies and prior natural immunity.

While the outcomes of acute COVID-19 have certainly improved since March 2020 in the general population and among patients with SARDs, an understanding of contemporary outcomes is critical for guiding the ongoing care of patients living with SARDs. SARS-CoV-2 vaccines are one effective measure to reduce the risk of infection and prevent severe infection but the humoral response to vaccination in people using certain immunosuppressants may be blunted and the response to vaccination is known to wane over time.32 33 Booster vaccines in people using immunosuppressants can reduce the risk of breakthrough infection and improve the humoral response.32 34 There are no clear guidelines regarding the optimal frequency of booster vaccinations in immunocompromised adults in the USA, though Australian and UK guidelines recommend considering updated vaccines every 6 months in immunocompromised adults.35 36 However, vaccine hesitancy remains a challenge, including in marginalised communities, and our findings reinforce the importance of maintaining updated COVID-19 vaccines in this high-risk population.37 38 While some of our observed associations (eg, race) are non-modifiable, an understanding of which patients are at high risk can direct the use of mitigation strategies that are resource-limited and identify groups who might benefit from more specific counselling. It is also known that more severe acute COVID-19 infections are associated with a higher risk of long COVID, including among patients with SARDs.39 40 Therefore, strategies to improve acute COVID-19 outcomes may also impact the risk of long COVID.

Since the beginning of the pandemic, use of CD20 inhibitors and/or glucocorticoids has been consistently identified as a risk factor for severe COVID-19 outcomes.6 14 21 41 42 Our findings illustrate that these associations have persisted even during the Omicron era. CD20 inhibitor use and glucocorticoid use, particularly at higher doses, have also been associated with impaired response to the SARS-CoV-2 vaccine, which may have contributed, in part, to the associations noted here. However, we did not collect data on the use of these medications at the time of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination. Among CD20 inhibitor users, the timing of vaccination in relation to B cell repopulation and infusions may be important to maximising vaccine response.43 44 In addition to identifying strategies that may improve vaccine effectiveness in patients using these treatments, patients using these treatments may also benefit from pre-exposure prophylaxis.45,47

We also found significantly higher odds of hospitalisation among self-reported Black race (compared with self-reported White race) in our primary, subgroup and sensitivity analyses. Disparities in outcomes have been noted since the start of the pandemic.28 48 The reasons behind these disparities are likely multifactorial, with some data indicating that differential exposures and healthcare access may impact outcomes more than differences in comorbidities or other underlying conditions.48 Additional work is needed to understand the collective impact of social determinants of health on outcomes in individuals with SARDs.

Our findings of higher odds of hospitalisation with greater comorbidity burden and with multiple individual comorbidities are also consistent with data seen in the general population. Multiple comorbidities—particularly renal impairment, cardiovascular disease, diabetes and obesity—have been found to be associated with increased risk of worse COVID-19 outcomes.14 15 21 29 Multimorbidity and different combinations of comorbidities are associated with even greater odds of severe COVID-19; one study found that the combination of diabetes and chronic renal impairment was associated with fivefold higher odds of severe outcome.29 Multiple prior studies have demonstrated increased risk of severe complications, including death in those with interstitial lung disease.17 49 Possible contributors to these findings include the possibility of viral infection exacerbating underlying interstitial lung disease as well as individuals with interstitial lung disease being poor candidates for mechanical ventilation, and thus not being offered mechanical ventilation in the setting of severe disease.49

Our study has several strengths. First, we systematically identified patients with prevalent SARDs and confirmed COVID-19 infection in a large healthcare system. Second, we included data from individuals who had SARS-CoV-2 tests done within the healthcare system as well as those who reported positive home tests in order to capture those with more mild infections who did not present for care as a result of COVID-19 infection. Third, we manually confirmed key exposures of interest, including immunosuppression and other disease- and treatment-specific factors, and we confirmed both details of hospitalisation and determined whether hospitalisation was due to COVID-19 versus unrelated. Fourth, the cause of death and its association with COVID-19 was determined by manual chart review by a study physician.

Despite these strengths, our study has several limitations. First, the denominator is likely an underestimate as many individuals may have had mild infections and either not performed tests and/or not reported a positive home test to their provider. As such, it is difficult to interpret the absolute rate of hospitalisation observed in our cohort. However, we note that the hospitalisation rate in our cohort is likely higher than the hospitalisation rate in the general population.50 Second, though our findings remained robust in multivariable adjusted analyses and in sensitivity analyses meant to further address potential confounding by indication, unmeasured confounding is possible in retrospective cohort studies of this nature. Reassuringly, our findings were consistent with risk factors observed earlier in the pandemic and fit with our understanding of the biology of COVID-19. Third, we limited the analysis to all patients identified to have COVID-19 during the study period. While we considered analysing all patients with SARDs in our system, the underestimation of mild or unreported COVID-19 cases limited this approach. Fourth, while we had detailed clinical data available to determine relatedness of COVID-19 to hospitalisations, the relative contribution of COVID-19 to the outcomes may have varied. Fifth, there may be some misclassification on covariates due to factors such as medication adherence and vaccination outside of the state (ie, vaccinations that may not be captured within our EHR), though this would typically bias towards the null. Finally, we examined a single geographic area with limited diversity, so our findings may not be generalisable.

In summary, we found associations between certain demographic factors (eg, older age, Black race, smoking), greater comorbidity burden, as well as certain medications, including CD20 inhibitors and systemic glucocorticoids, with higher odds of hospitalisation for COVID-19 infection among individuals with SARDs during the Omicron era. The odds of hospitalisation have remained roughly stable over calendar time since 2022, indicating that individuals with SARDs remain at risk of hospitalisation for COVID-19. Greater number and more recent SARS-CoV-2 vaccination were associated with lower odds of hospitalisation, indicating that ongoing mitigation measures including updated vaccinations and pre-exposure prophylaxis should be considered.
